title: SilverCurrent - Concurrency & Tokenflow Profiling
summary: Initial discovery for latency and throughput targets. Customer needs p95 <= 350ms for short responses, streaming for real-time UIs, and steady token/sec during peak bursts. Discussion covered Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, KV/prefix caching, batching, fallback model variants, and a pilot benchmarking plan.
next_steps: Redwood: share trimmed benchmarking worksheet and example load script (Priya)
Customer: provide example request/response size distribution and peak concurrency profile (Alex/Samira)
Schedule 2-hour pilot kickoff to run token/sec streaming tests next week
Redwood: provide security checklist for Private deploy evaluation
action_items: Priya Nair: prepare a 3-node Dedicated benchmark run template and cost estimate (due 2026-06-05)
Alex Morgan: export 48h of production traffic histogram and example prompts (due 2026-06-04)
Ben Cho: confirm whether KV caching of user histories is allowed (due 2026-06-03)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (CTO, SilverCurrent), Samira Ortiz (SRE), Ben Cho (ML Eng)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Alex: Good, thanks. Excited to chat — we want to validate a couple of p95 and streaming assumptions for our real-time analytics UI.
[00:14] Priya: Awesome. Maybe to kick off do you want to share the top-level SLA you're aiming for and typical payload sizes? Even ballpark numbers help.
[00:23] Samira: Yeah, top-level p95 target is 350 milliseconds for short completions (under ~150 tokens). For longer generation flows we can tolerate higher p95, up to 1.2s for 1k tokens. Concurrency: typical steady concurrency is 40, but peaks up to ~550 concurrent streams during promos.
[00:40] Ben: Token sizes vary — most requests are 30–120 tokens prompt, responses 50–300 tokens. We do a lot of streaming so p50/p95 during token emission matters a lot.
[00:52] Jordan: Nice. That gives a good shape. Quick qual: are you leaning Hosted, Dedicated, or Private now, or evaluating all three?
[00:59] Alex: We're evaluating. Prefer hosted for speed to market but worried about cost and data residency; Dedicated looks like a potential middle ground if latency is consistent; Private only if we hit compliance gates.
[01:13] Priya: Makes sense. On the latency side, p95 for short completions is dominated by model latency (kernel path) plus network hop to the cluster. With Redwood Hosted we can often hit sub-200ms p95 for small models on optimized kernels; for larger foot- print models it moves. For streaming you care about per-chunk latency — our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache, which helps with repeated prefixes.
[01:40] Samira: Can you expand on KV cache? We currently keep user context on Redis and re-send or reference handles — curious how Redwood does it.
[01:48] Priya: Sure. We maintain a token-level KV cache across requests so if you have repeated context — think user system prompt or session history — we can reuse past KV attention states so generation time for subsequent calls skips recomputing early layers. That reduces token/sec and latency. Sometimes transcription or notes from our internal logs show 'KV cash' instead of cache, ha.
[02:09] Jordan: Ha, yes KV cash.
[02:12] Ben: That could change cost a lot if we do long-ish dialogs. Do you expose guarantees around cache hit rates or is that workload specific?
[02:20] Priya: Hit rate is workload specific but we provide tooling that simulates your session patterns and estimates hit rate and latency improvements. For planning we can run a short replay of sample traffic and show the delta.
[02:31] Alex: For concurrency and bursts, our chief worry is token bursts from scheduled sync jobs that fan out. They would translate to a 10–15 minute spike at ~500 concurrent streaming requests. If the provider throttles or queues too aggressively that kills UX.
[02:45] Jordan: Understood. Our Dedicated offering gives you reserved capacity and predictable throughput; for bursts we support controlled auto-burst lanes or cross-region fallback to keep requests live. For Hosted we have auto-scaling but at extreme spikes there may be higher p95 unless you opt for a capacity reservation or pin a model variant.
[03:03] Samira: What about cold starts for Worker nodes, and the effect on p95?
[03:07] Priya: Cold starts are small for our runtime — typically tens to low hundreds of ms for worker spin-up depending on model size. But in steady state p95 should be dominated by inference path. We also do proactive warm pools for Dedicated.
[03:20] Ben: We use mixed model sizes, sometimes a gzipped 13B and sometimes 70B for heavier tasks. Are you recommending quantized variants for Dedicated?
[03:29] Priya: Yes, quantization often gives big gains in throughput and memory. For 13B and 70B we have validated int8 and 4-bit paths — tradeoff is small accuracy delta; Redwood Optimize can run eval prompts to detect regressions. For strict accuracy we can run A/B between variants.
[03:45] Alex: If we ran a pilot what does that look like? We want to capture p95 streaming per-token latency, tokens/sec sustained, and end-to-end from our browser to observer.
[03:55] Jordan: Typical pilot is 2 steps — a lightweight profiling run using a sample of your requests to estimate model variants and batching configs, then a short stress test simulating bursts at target concurrency. We provide scripts (JMeter-like) and a small runner. Priya can lay out specifics.
[04:08] Priya: For streaming per-token latency we instrument at the chunk emit point. We'll ask you to provide a distribution of prompt lengths and preferred chunk size. Then we'll test at steady-state 40 concurrent and then ramp to 550 concurrent over 10 minutes to mirror your promo pattern.
[04:23] Samira: What's the expected tokens/sec drop as concurrency increases? Any heuristics?
[04:27] Priya: It depends on batching policy. With aggressive continuous batching throughput increases but single-request latency can suffer slightly. For example, on a 13B quantized model we might see single-stream token latency ~15–20ms/chunk at low concurrency; at high concurrency with batching overall tokens/sec increases and per-token latency stays roughly stable if you tune batch size and max latency SLO. If your p95 target is strict, we might advise Dedicated with reserved lanes.
[04:51] Ben: Question on network: would colocating inference in our cloud region materially help? We run primarily in eu-west-1.
[04:58] Jordan: Yes. Latency to client is the client->region hop. With Redwood Private or Dedicated deployed in eu-west-1 you'll remove cross-region hops. Hosted can also route to eu region but Dedicated/Private gives more control.
[05:10] Alex: Security flags — we may need SOC2-type logs and SAML SSO for admin. Also KMS integration is a must.
[05:18] Priya: We support SAML/RBAC, KMS, and detailed audit logs for Dedicated and Private. Hosted has SOC2 controls and customer-managed KMS for enterprise plans. We'll drop the security checklist after call.
[05:28] Samira: For the telemetry we want token-level cost breakdown by model and an alert if p95 increases 20% from baseline.
[05:35] Jordan: Redwood Console supports token-level cost and per-model p95 dashboards. Alerts can be wired to PagerDuty or Slack.
[05:41] Ben: On pricing, ballpark numbers between Hosted and Dedicated for our profile?
[05:45] Jordan: Hosted is straightforward per-token + streaming unit. Dedicated has committed monthly price for a GPU pool plus lower per-token engine cost; for your steady 40 and peak patterns we'd model both — Priya will include sample math in the benchmark worksheet.
[05:58] Alex: OK great. Can you walk through a short demo of how you'll measure p95 for streaming? Even rough sequence.
[06:04] Priya: Sure. Sequence: 1) ingest sample prompts, 2) reproduce client chunking behavior (chunk size 64 tokens), 3) spin up test agents in eu-west-1, 4) run a steady test for 30 minutes to characterize p50/p95/p99, 5) run an escalation burst. We'll capture server-side timing and client-perceived timings.
[06:28] Jordan: And we'll attach the small load generator and a sample dashboard template.
[06:33] Samira: Are there guardrails to prevent the test from affecting production? Our sync jobs run in production buckets.
[06:38] Priya: We recommend running tests against a shadowed replica or test endpoint. If you want to run against hosted we can create a sandbox project and isolated keys so there's no production impact.
[06:48] Alex: About fallback policies — if Dedicated is saturated do you automatically fallback to Hosted? How's cross-model fallback handled?
[06:55] Jordan: We have routing policies. You can configure automatic fallback to a compatible model variant (e.g., quantized or lower size) or to Hosted as long as data residency/privacy rules allow it. We'll show an example policy for graceful degradation.
[07:07] Ben: Any limits on streaming chunk size? We currently emit chunks of ~64 tokens every 200ms.
[07:13] Priya: That's fine; chunk interval and size is completely configurable. Smaller chunks increase overhead but improve perceived latency. We'll measure tradeoffs in the pilot.
[07:24] Samira: For the high burst scenario do you recommend queuing or immediate 429?
[07:29] Jordan: UX dependent. If low-latency is critical prefer reserved capacity or burst lanes; if cost matters you can implement adaptive throttling with graceful degrade messaging. We can instrument a 429->retry with jitter policy.
[07:42] Alex: Good. Any gotchas with second-order effects like KV cache thrash during multitenant workloads?
[07:48] Priya: Yes, cache locality matters. If you have highly unique session contexts cache hit rate goes down. We can simulate churn and recommend per-tenant cache partitioning for Dedicated/Private.
[07:58] Ben: For the demo/pilot timeline — can we do initial profiling this week and stress test next week?
[08:03] Jordan: Sounds feasible. Priya, is the 48-hour window for sample logs enough?
[08:07] Priya: Yes, 24–72h of representative traffic is ideal. Alex if you can send a CSV with request lengths and timestamps we'll sketch the test.
[08:15] Alex: We'll do that. Anything else on the telemetry side?
[08:19] Samira: One last on regional failover — if eu-east has an outage and traffic routes to us-west do you have automatic fanout?
[08:26] Jordan: We support multi-region routing and can prioritize locality; fallback is configurable. For strict SLOs you can set regional failover thresholds.
[08:35] Ben: Ok thanks.
[08:37] Jordan: Let's recap real quick. Action items: Redwood to send benchmark worksheet, example load script, and security checklist. Customer to provide traffic histogram and confirm KV caching permissions. Pilot kickoff next week — Jordan will schedule a 2-hour slot.
[08:55] Alex: Sounds good. Appreciate the thoroughness.
[09:00] Jordan: Great, we'll follow up with the links and calendar invite. Thanks everyone.

Meeting end.

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-hearings (KV cache flagged as KV cash in auto-transcript). Some timestamps approximate as Fireflies transcription segments.
